newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya hotel group sale may boost Nairobi bourse.
newsitem.headline: Kenya hotel group sale may boost Nairobi bourse.

text.p: The Kenyan government will sell 23.3 percent of its stake in the luxury Serena Lodges & Hotel chain from March 24 in a move officials say will increase investor potential at the Nairobi bourse and emphasise commitment to privatisation.

The 23.3 percent stake, or 9.03 million shares, will be sold at a price of 13 shillings (23 U.S. cents) per share. The offer will open on March 24 and close on April 14, Serena Hotels Chief Executive Mahmud Jan Mohamed told a news briefing on Thursday.

The shares are part of a 33.3 percent stake held by the government tourist agency Kenya Tourism Development Corp (KTDC) in Tourism Promotion Services, the Aga Khan firm that runs the Serena Hotels & Lodges Ltd. It retains the 10 percent balance.
The Serena announcement came on the same day as Regent Undervalued Assets Africa, incorporated in Cayman Islands, became the first international fund to be listed on the bourse.
Regent will be listed simultaneously on the Dublin and Botswana stock exchanges and seeks to obtain capital growth by investing in a range of undervalued opportunities in Africa.

"The two listings improve potential and liquidity," said John Munge, managing director of brokerage company Shah, Munge & Partners. "It is an affirmation of government commitment to privatisation and will enhance overall economic growth."

Serena owns five luxury hotels in Nairobi, Mombasa and the game reserves of Masai Mara, Amboseli and Samburu, with a total of 590 rooms. It posted profit after tax of 41.22 million shillings in the year ending 31 December 1996 compared to 50.15 million shillings in the previous year.
Serena blamed the lower earnings in 1996 on its refurbishing of the Nairobi Serena Hotel, considered a gem in Nairobi.

The Serena flotation comes after the success seen in the sale of national carrier Kenya Airways as well as sale of part of the government's holding in National Bank of Kenya and Kenya Commercial Bank last year.

Munge forecast a boom on the Nairobi Stock Exchange in 1997 with growth of 30-50 percent. But he said this was conditional on the central bank checking money supply and ensuring that inflation did not rise to "unreasonable" levels.

Munge said brokers hoped that a drought, declared a national disaster by Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, would pass relatively quickly because it had a devastating effect on low-income earners, on whom the bourse now relies for growth.
Kenya's three-months overall annualised inflation rose to 14.7 percent in February from 9.4 percent in January on rising food prices blamed on drought in this East African country.
"We still have cheap pickings on this stock exchange. So this should be a good year," Munge told Reuters.
Serena and Regent bring to 60 the total number of companies listed on the Nairobi Stock Exchange.
A second tranche of $37 million of an agreed $220 million in an International Monetary Fund soft-loans programme has been delayed by concerns that revolve mainly around privatisation.
The central bank said on Tuesday that Kenya's gross domestic product growth was only 4.8 percent last year from 4.9 percent in 1995 and less than 6.0 percent forecast earlier.
